content: Rhubarb is a perennial plant that grows from thick, short rhizomes and belongs to the genus Rheum, which is part of the family Polygonaceae. This family also includes plants such as dock, sorrel, knotweeds, knotgrasses, and buckwheat. The plant features large, somewhat triangular leaf blades that are supported by long, fleshy petioles. Its flowers are small, greenish-white, and grow in large, compound leafy inflorescences. Although rhubarb is technically an herb, it is often used in culinary contexts as a fruit. In the United States, it was classified as a vegetable until the 1940s, when customs officials reclassified it as a fruit based on its culinary use. Rhubarb is native to Asia and is believed to have been used historically by Mongolian tribes, particularly the Tatars of the Gobi region. It has also grown wild along the banks of the Volga River for centuries, possibly introduced there by Eurasian tribes such as the Scythians, Huns, Magyars, or Mongols. While rhubarb has a long history as a medicinal plant in traditional Chinese medicine, its use as a food is relatively recent, first recorded in 17th-century England after sugar became more affordable for the general population. Today, rhubarb is cultivated in many regions, primarily for its fleshy petioles, commonly referred to as rhubarb sticks or stalks. In temperate climates, rhubarb is one of the first food plants ready for harvest, typically in mid to late spring (April/May in the Northern Hemisphere, October/November in the Southern Hemisphere). The petioles can be cooked in various ways, often yielding a tart sauce when stewed, which can be sweetened and used as a filling for pies, tarts, and crumbles. This common culinary use has led to the slang term pie plant for rhubarb. In Germany, the term Rhabarber is similarly used. Rhubarb is also commonly cooked with strawberries to make jam and can be used to produce wine or as an ingredient in cakes. Historically, in parts of the United Kingdom and Sweden, children would enjoy a simple treat of tender rhubarb sticks dipped in sugar. In the UK, the first rhubarb of the year is often grown in dark sheds under candlelight in the Rhubarb Triangle region of Wakefield, Leeds, and Morley. In warmer climates, rhubarb can grow year-round, but in colder climates, the above-ground parts of the plant die back completely during winter and regrow from the root in early spring. Rhubarb can also be forced to grow early by raising the local temperature, often achieved by placing an upturned bucket over the emerging shoots. Medicinally, rhubarb has been used as a strong laxative and for its astringent effects on the mucous membranes of the mouth and nasal cavity. The genus Rheum includes approximately 60 extant species. Among the wild species, the most commonly used in cooking are Garden Rhubarb (R. rhabarbarum) and R. rhaponticum, the latter often referred to as False Rhubarb despite being a true rhubarb. Cultivated varieties grown for consumption are typically recognized as Rheum x hybridum in the Royal Horticultural Society's list of plant names. The medicinal drug rheum is derived from the rhizomes and roots of another species, R. officinale or Medicinal Rhubarb, which is also native to Asia, as is Turkey Rhubarb (R. palmatum). Another species, Sikkim Rhubarb (R. nobile), is native to the Himalayas. Additionally, species of Rheum have been recorded as larval food plants for various Lepidoptera species, including the Brown-tail, Buff Ermine, Cabbage Moth, Large Yellow Underwing, The Nutmeg, Setaceous Hebrew Character, and Turnip Moth. Rhubarb leaves contain toxic substances, including oxalic acid, which is both corrosive and nephrotoxic. The estimated median lethal dose (LD50) for pure oxalic acid is approximately 375 mg/kg body weight, or about 25 grams for a 65 kg (140 lb) human. However, consuming a lethal dose of oxalic acid from rhubarb leaves would require ingesting an unlikely five kilograms of the extremely sour leaves. Additionally, the leaves are believed to contain another unidentified toxin. The petioles, in contrast, contain much lower levels of oxalic acid, especially when harvested before mid-June in the Northern Hemisphere, though they can still cause a slightly rough sensation on the teeth. The roots and stems of rhubarb are rich in anthraquinones, such as emodin and rhein, which have cathartic and laxative properties. These compounds can occasionally lead to the misuse of rhubarb as a slimming agent. Anthraquinones are yellow or orange in color and may tint the urine. The word rhubarb has also been used in various non-botanical contexts. In acting, a crowd of extras might repeatedly shout rhubarb out of sync to create the effect of general background noise or hubbub. This usage has led to the term rhubarb being associated with superfluous or irrelevant text in speech or writing, as well as general chatter among chorus or extra actors. In American English, the equivalent term is walla. The word rhubarb has also come to denote a loud argument, particularly in baseball, where it refers to a fight involving multiple players, such as a bench-clearing brawl. In the 1989 film Batman, the Joker (played by Jack Nicholson) uses the phrase never rub another man's rhubarb as a warning to Bruce Wayne (Michael Keaton) to stay away from their mutual love interest, Vicki Vale (Kim Basinger). The phrase out in the rhubarb patch can describe a remote or far-reaching area, reflecting the plant's traditional placement at the edges of gardens in less desirable or untended spaces. The term Donkey Rhubarb refers to Japanese knotweed and is sometimes used as slang for cannabis in certain parts of Canada, replacing terms like weed or pot. Rhubarb is also humorously referenced in the fictional product Be-Bop-A-Re-Bop Rhubarb Pie in the radio program A Prairie Home Companion. In the 2006 film adaptation of the program, rhubarb itself is mentioned, including an explanation of the origin of its name.
